g11-physics-up3-t1.overview: When acceleration is constant, four equations — the SUVAT equations — solve every straight-line motion problem: cars braking, trains starting, rockets launching. Master the sign convention and the equation selection, and 1D kinematics becomes mechanical.
objectives: Apply the four SUVAT equations fluently with correct signs
Choose the right equation by spotting the omitted variable
Solve multi-stage motion problems (accelerate → cruise → brake)
Interpret stopping distance, reaction time and relative motion in 1D
g11-physics-up3-t1.simple: Constant acceleration gives you four cheat codes. v = u + at (velocity after t), s = ut + ½at² (where you end up), v² = u² + 2as (no time needed), s = ½(u+v)t (average velocity × time). Write u, v, a, s, t, list the three you know and the one you want — the leftover letter tells you which equation. Signs matter: pick + for the direction of travel, and braking becomes a = negative.
g11-physics-up3-t1.detailed:
Setup: motion along one line with constant a. Variables: initial velocity u, final v, acceleration a, displacement s, time t. (Grade 11 writes them as u/v/a/s/t — the 'SUVAT' set.) All are signed: choose +x as the direction of initial motion or the downward direction — then stick with it through the whole problem.

The four equations (each omits exactly one variable):
1. v = u + at (no s)
2. s = ut + ½at² (no v)
3. v² = u² + 2as (no t)
4. s = ½(u + v)t (no a)
Derivation insight: (1) is the definition of a; (4) is average velocity × time (valid ONLY for constant a); (2) and (3) follow by substitution.

Selection strategy: list knowns + unknown; the equation that omits the variable you neither have nor need is the one-liner solution.

Braking & stopping: v = 0 at stop. Stopping distance = thinking distance (reaction time × speed, constant velocity) + braking distance (v² = u² + 2as with a = −deceleration). Doubling speed QUADRUPLES braking distance — the physics behind speed limits.

Multi-stage problems: split at each change of acceleration; the final velocity of stage 1 is the initial velocity of stage 2; total displacement = sum of stages. Draw a v–t sketch first.

Relative motion in 1D: velocity of A relative to B: v_AB = v_A − v_B (signed). Two cars at 80 and 60 km/h same direction: closing speed 20 km/h. Opposite directions: speeds ADD for approach.

Free-fall preview: near Earth's surface a = −g = −9.8 m/s² whenever an object moves under gravity alone — the same four equations apply (next lesson's vertical motion is just SUVAT with a = g).

keyTerms.def: The five constant-acceleration variables u, v, a, s, t and the four equations linking them.
Chosen + direction; all vectors get signed values consistently.
Acceleration opposing velocity — negative a under our convention.
Speed × reaction time, before brakes bite.
v²=u²+2as stopping distance under maximum deceleration.
v_AB = v_A − v_B: velocity as seen from B.

formulas.name: Velocity–time
formulas.meaning: Final velocity after time t at constant acceleration.

formulas.name: Velocity–displacement
formulas.meaning: Links speeds to distance, no clock needed.
formulas.when: Time unknown and unwanted — braking problems.
formulas.example: u=20, a=−5: stop distance s = 400/10 = 40 m.

formulas.name: Average velocity form
formulas.meaning: Displacement = mean speed × time (constant a only).

workedExamples.problem: A car accelerates uniformly from rest at 2.5 m/s² for 12 s. Find (a) final velocity, (b) distance travelled, (c) verify with the average-velocity equation.
workedExamples.formula: v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; s = ½(u+v)t.
workedExamples.answer: v = 30 m/s (108 km/h), s = 180 m — two independent routes agree.

workedExamples.problem: A bus travelling at 15 m/s brakes uniformly and stops in 25 m. Find the deceleration and the braking time.
workedExamples.formula: v² = u² + 2as (no t); then s = ½(u+v)t.
workedExamples.answer: Deceleration 4.5 m/s², stopped in 3.3 s — hard but achievable braking.

workedExamples.problem: A train accelerates at 0.6 m/s² from rest for 40 s, cruises for 2 minutes, then brakes uniformly to a stop in 60 s. Find total distance.
workedExamples.formula: Stage analysis; v of stage 1 = u of stage 2.
workedExamples.answer: 4.08 km — always split multi-stage motion at each acceleration change.

workedExamples.problem: Reaction time is 0.6 s. Compare total stopping distances at 15 m/s and 30 m/s for a car with maximum deceleration 6 m/s².
workedExamples.answer: Doubling speed more than TRIPLES stopping distance (93/28 ≈ 3.4×) — braking distance scales with v², thinking distance with v.

workedExamples.problem: Car A at 90 km/h approaches car B at 60 km/h head-on. Find their relative speed in m/s, and the time to collision if they start 500 m apart.
workedExamples.formula: v_AB = v_A − v_B (signed); closing speed = sum of magnitudes.
workedExamples.answer: Relative speed 41.7 m/s (150 km/h); collision in ~12 s — head-on closing speeds add, which is why head-on crashes are so severe.

commonMistakes: Mixing km/h with m/s without converting (×1000/3600 = ÷3.6).
Forgetting the negative sign on deceleration — then 'solving' v = u + at with a = +5 for braking.
Using s = ut + ½at² with v instead of u (letter confusion).
Applying average-velocity equation s = ½(u+v)t when acceleration is NOT constant.
Stopping-distance panic: forgetting thinking distance is part of the total.
Relative velocity sign errors: same direction → subtract; opposite → add.
applications: Road safety engineering: sight distances, speed limits and crash statistics all come from v² scaling.
Train and elevator scheduling: acceleration phases determine journey times.
Sports: sprinter start analysis (first 30 m is near-constant acceleration).
Aviation: catapult launches and arrestor-deck landings are SUVAT extremes.
Rocketry staging preview: burn-phase acceleration then coast.
g11-physics-up3-t1.summary: Constant a ⇒ four SUVAT equations, each omitting one variable — pick by what you lack. Signs: one convention, kept throughout. Braking: v² = u² + 2as; stopping distance = reaction + v²/2a (quadratic in speed). Multi-stage: chain stages via shared velocity. Relative 1D: subtract signed velocities.

steps: List u, v, a, s, t (knowns + target)
Find the equation omitting the unused letter

g11-physics-up3-t2.overview: Graphs are motion in pictures: the slope of a position–time graph is velocity, the slope of a velocity–time graph is acceleration, and the area under v–t is displacement. Reading these three operations lets you decode — and design — any constant-acceleration journey.
objectives: Sketch and interpret s–t, v–t and a–t graphs for standard motions
Extract velocity from s–t gradients and acceleration from v–t gradients
Compute displacement as area under v–t (including signed areas)
Convert between graph representations (s–t ↔ v–t ↔ a–t)
g11-physics-up3-t2.simple: Three golden rules: SLOPE of distance graph = speed. SLOPE of velocity graph = acceleration. AREA under velocity graph = displacement. Straight line on s–t = constant speed; curve getting steeper = speeding up. On v–t: flat = cruise, slope = accelerate, area = how far. Below the axis? Moving backwards — area counts negative.
g11-physics-up3-t2.detailed:
Position–time (s–t): gradient = instantaneous velocity. Straight line → constant v (steeper = faster). Horizontal → at rest. Curving upward (gradient increasing) → accelerating; inflection → velocity maximum. To find v at an instant: draw the TANGENT and measure its slope (Δs/Δt using a long triangle).

Velocity–time (v–t): gradient = acceleration; area between curve and time axis = displacement. Constant v → rectangle area (s = vt). Uniform a → triangle/trapezium area (s = ½(u+v)t — the equations ARE the areas). Negative velocity → area below axis → displacement decreases (object returning). Total distance = sum of |areas|; net displacement = signed sum.

Acceleration–time (a–t): area = change in velocity (Δv). Constant a → rectangle. Jerk (rate of change of a) is the a–t slope — rarely needed but conceptually the third layer.

Standard shapes to know cold:
• Rest: s–t flat, v–t on zero line.
• Constant v: s–t sloped line, v–t flat above axis, a–t zero.
• Constant +a from rest: s–t upward parabola, v–t sloped line from origin, a–t flat positive.
• Braking to stop: v–t sloped line DOWN to axis; area = stopping distance.
• Return journey: v–t dips below axis; signed areas cancel at the start point.

Reading stories from graphs (exam staple): describe a v–t piecewise: '0–20 s accelerate uniformly to 15 m/s; 20–60 s cruise; 60–75 s decelerate to rest; 75–90 s reverse at up to 5 m/s…' — every segment gets slope (a) and area (s) numbers.

Sketching skill: given a scenario, axes labelled with units and key values marked (not to scale, but proportionally sensible) earns full marks — mark intercepts, turning points and axis crossings.

keyTerms.def: Rise/run of a line — here: s–t → v, v–t → a.
Line touching a curve at one point — gives the instantaneous rate.
Area below the time axis counts negative (reverse motion).
Net signed area vs total |area| under v–t.
Signature of constant nonzero acceleration.

formulas.name: Graph operations
formulas.formula: v = ds/dt (slope) | a = dv/dt (slope) | Δs = ∫v dt (area) | Δv = ∫a dt (area)
formulas.meaning: Slope differentiates one graph into the next; area integrates back down.
formulas.when: Any motion graph — the three operations connect s–t, v–t, a–t.
formulas.example: v–t triangle 0→10 m/s over 5 s: a = 2 m/s², s = ½×10×5 = 25 m.

workedExamples.problem: A v–t graph: rises linearly 0→20 m/s in 8 s, flat for 12 s, falls to 0 in 10 s. Find (a) the two accelerations, (b) total displacement, (c) sketch the matching a–t graph.
workedExamples.answer: +2.5 then −2 m/s²; 420 m total; a–t is a two-step rectangle pattern.

workedExamples.problem: An object's s–t graph is a parabola s = 3t². Find its velocity at t = 4 s using the tangent idea, and confirm with SUVAT.
workedExamples.formula: Tangent slope; compare with s = ut + ½at².
workedExamples.substitution: Tangent at t = 4: take points t = 3.9 → 4.1: s(4.1) − s(3.9) = 50.43 − 45.63 = 4.8 over 0.2 s → slope ≈ 24 m/s. Matching: ½a = 3 → a = 6 m/s², u = 0; v = at = 6×4.
workedExamples.answer: 24 m/s — the tangent slope and v = at agree; parabola coefficient half = acceleration.

workedExamples.problem: A particle's v–t graph is +10 m/s for 0–5 s, then −5 m/s for 5–9 s. Find (a) total distance, (b) final displacement from start.
workedExamples.formula: Distance = Σ|area|; displacement = Σ signed area.
workedExamples.answer: 70 m travelled, ending 30 m from start — the difference between |area| and signed area.

workedExamples.problem: Describe the motion shown by an s–t graph that rises steeply, flattens to horizontal for 10 s, then descends with a gentler constant slope back to the axis.
workedExamples.substitution: Steep rise = fast constant velocity away; flat = stationary 10 s; gentle descent = slower constant velocity returning.
workedExamples.calculation: Return slope magnitude < outbound slope → return speed lower; ends at origin → displacement zero overall.
workedExamples.answer: Out fast, rest, back slow — a complete round trip with a stopover.

commonMistakes: Reading a v–t graph's HEIGHT as distance (it's speed — distance is the AREA).
Confusing the two slopes: s–t slope = v; v–t slope = a.
Ignoring negative areas: displacement ≠ total distance when motion reverses.
Measuring tangent slope from the axes intercept instead of Δ(vertical)/Δ(horizontal) along the tangent.
Thinking a horizontal v–t line means 'at rest' — it means constant velocity (rest is v = 0 specifically).
Sketching s–t for constant acceleration as a straight line — it's a parabola.
applications: Car crash analysis: skid marks + v–t reconstruction give pre-braking speed.
Heart monitors and seismographs are slope/area machines (rate and total effect).
Flight data recorders store v–t profiles; ATC reads them after incidents.
Sports video analysis produces s–t curves to compare sprinters' acceleration phases.
Electricity meters integrate power over time (area) — same mathematics, kWh.
g11-physics-up3-t2.summary: Slope chain: s–t → v, v–t → a. Area chain: a–t → Δv, v–t → Δs (signed!). Straight = uniform; parabola = constant a; tangent = instantaneous. Distance = Σ|areas|, displacement = Σ signed areas. Every SUVAT equation is just an area statement in disguise.

g11-physics-up3-t3.overview: Throw anything up and gravity writes the script: a constant 9.8 m/s² downward, symmetric rise and fall, and a velocity that passes through zero at the very top. Vertical motion is SUVAT with one fixed acceleration — and the classic exam favourite.
objectives: Apply SUVAT to objects thrown upward or dropped (a = −g)
Explain why v = 0 at maximum height while a = −g still
Use the symmetry of rise and fall to shortcut problems
Solve multi-object and round-trip vertical problems
g11-physics-up3-t3.simple: Up or down, gravity pulls at 9.8 m/s² — always. Throw a ball up at 20 m/s: it loses 9.8 m/s every second, stops dead at the top (v = 0, but STILL accelerating down!), then speeds up coming back. Same height on the way up and down = same speed. Time up = time down (no air resistance). Just use the four equations with a = −9.8 and a consistent +up convention.
g11-physics-up3-t3.detailed:
Convention: take +y upward; then a = −g = −9.8 m/s² for ANY free object (thrown up, down, or dropped) — gravity doesn't care about your throw direction. (Or take +down for drops; either works if consistent.)

Key facts:
• At maximum height: v = 0 INSTANTANEOUSLY, but a = −g unchanged — the velocity is passing through zero, not resting.
• Symmetry: launch speed = return speed at the same height; t_up = t_down; speed at height h is identical going up and down (v² = u² − 2gΔy has two roots ±v).

Standard equations (up + convention): v = u − gt; y = ut − ½gt²; v² = u² − 2gy. Dropped from rest: y = ½gt² (down + convention).

Problem archetypes:
1. Max height: set v = 0 → h = u²/2g.
2. Total air time (returns to launch): y = 0 → t = 2u/g.
3. Time at a given height: quadratic → often TWO times (up-pass and down-pass).
4. Two objects (one dropped, one thrown later): write both y(t), set equal, solve.
5. From a cliff: launch point ≠ landing point; displacement = −(cliff height) with +up.

Velocity–time picture: a straight line of slope −g crossing the axis at the top — the triangle above the axis (rise) mirrors the triangle below (fall); equal areas = equal up/down distances.

Air resistance reality check: with drag, the descent takes LONGER than the ascent and return speed < launch speed — the symmetry breaks. Grade 11 problems are vacuum unless stated.

keyTerms.def: Motion under gravity alone (a = g downward), even while moving upward.
9.8 m/s² (≈10 in estimates) — gravitational field strength / fall acceleration.
Highest point: v = 0, a = −g.
Equal times and mirrored speeds for up vs down legs.
A height is crossed twice — once up, once down.

formulas.name: Vertical SUVAT (+up)
formulas.formula: v = u − gt | y = ut − ½gt² | v² = u² − 2gy
formulas.meaning: The three constant-acceleration equations with a = −g.
formulas.when: Any throw up or down, ignoring air resistance.

formulas.name: Maximum height
formulas.meaning: Peak height of a vertical throw (from v = 0).

workedExamples.problem: A stone is thrown straight up at 24.5 m/s. Find (a) max height, (b) time to top, (c) total time to return, (d) velocity when it returns to hand.
workedExamples.formula: h = u²/2g; t_up = u/g; t_total = 2u/g; symmetry.
workedExamples.answer: 30.6 m high, 2.5 s up, 5 s total, returns at 24.5 m/s downward — perfect symmetry.

workedExamples.problem: From a 45 m cliff, a ball is thrown upward at 10 m/s. When does it hit the ground below? (Take +up, launch y = 0, ground y = −45.)
workedExamples.answer: ≈ 4.2 s. (The negative root is the mirror-time fiction — reject it.)

workedExamples.problem: A flowerpot falls off a roof 20 m up. At the same instant, a ball is thrown upward from the ground at 12 m/s. Do they meet? If so, when and where?
workedExamples.answer: Yes — at 1.67 s, 6.4 m above ground. (Both fall at the same rate, so their relative motion is uniform!)

workedExamples.problem: At what times is a ball thrown up at 19.6 m/s at a height of 14.7 m? Explain the two answers.
workedExamples.answer: 1 s going UP, 3 s coming DOWN — every height (below the apex) is crossed twice; apex at t = 2 s, h = 19.6 m.

commonMistakes: Saying a = 0 at the top — gravity never stops; only v is momentarily zero.
Sign chaos: throwing up with +down convention gives u = −24.5 — pick one convention and keep it.
Forgetting the ground may be BELOW launch (cliff problems: s is negative with +up).
Rejecting the second quadratic root when the question asks for BOTH times (up-pass and down-pass).
Using g = 9.8 in one step and 10 in another within the same problem.
Assuming return speed = launch speed when air resistance is explicitly present.
applications: Vertical jumps in sports: take-off speed from flight time (t_total = 2u/g inverted).
Fireworks: shell burst timing set to reach apex before exploding.
Construction: dropped-object hazard zones computed from fall time √(2h/g).
Rocketry: vertical ascent phase before gravity-turn.
Planetary science: measuring g on other worlds by throw-and-time experiments (Apollo hammer-feather drop).
g11-physics-up3-t3.summary: Vertical motion = SUVAT with a = −g (up +). Apex: v = 0, a = −g. Symmetry: equal up/down times and mirrored speeds; h = u²/2g, air time = 2u/g. Heights below apex crossed twice (two roots). Cliff problems: displacement ≠ zero. Two free-falling bodies have uniform relative motion.

The speed of a vertically thrown ball at half its maximum height equals half its launch speed.

g11-physics-up3-t4.overview: An object moving in a circle at constant SPEED is still accelerating — because its velocity DIRECTION changes every instant. That centripetal acceleration (v²/r) demands an inward force, and it explains everything from banked roads to satellites.
objectives: Explain why constant-speed circular motion is accelerated motion
Derive and apply a = v²/r = ω²r
Use period, frequency and angular velocity relationships
Identify centripetal forces in real situations and solve F = mv²/r problems
Describe conical pendulums and banked-turn applications
g11-physics-up3-t4.simple: Swing a stone on a string: it moves at constant speed but is ALWAYS accelerating — toward the centre. Why? Velocity is a vector; turning it counts as acceleration. The string's pull provides that inward (centripetal) acceleration: a = v²/r. Faster (v²) or tighter (÷r) turn = more acceleration needed. There is no outward 'centrifugal force' in the ground frame — cut the string and the stone flies off TANGENT, not outward.
g11-physics-up3-t4.detailed:
Why inward acceleration: velocity is tangent to the circle; constant turning means Δv always points inward (compare two nearby velocity vectors — the difference vector aims at the centre). Magnitude: a = v²/r. Direction: centre-seeking, perpendicular to v — so it changes direction of motion, never speed (work done = 0: F ⊥ d).

Cycle vocabulary: period T (seconds per revolution), frequency f = 1/T (Hz), angular velocity ω = 2π/T = 2πf (rad/s). Arc relations: s = rθ (θ in radians), v = rω. Then a = v²/r = ω²r = 4π²r/T².

Centripetal FORCE is a role, not a new force: ΣF_inward = mv²/r. The provider varies: tension (stone on string), friction (car rounding a bend), gravity (satellites, Moon), normal component (banked track), string horizontal component (conical pendulum). Free-body diagrams point real forces inward — never draw a mysterious outward force in an inertial frame.

Conical pendulum: string tension T at angle θ to vertical: T cosθ = mg, T sinθ = mv²/r → tanθ = v²/(rg). Faster spin → wider angle.

Banked curves: at design speed, normal force's horizontal component alone provides mv²/r: tanθ = v²/(rg) (frictionless ideal). Roads are banked so heavy vehicles can turn safely at speed; above design speed friction must add inward grip.

Vertical circles (loop-the-loop): at the top, gravity AND normal force point inward: mg + N = mv²/r. Minimum speed for contact: N = 0 → v_top = √(gr). Energy conservation supplies the bottom speed: v_bottom² = v_top² + 4gr.

Common frame confusion: 'centrifugal force' appears only in the rotating frame (a pseudo-force). In ground/inertial frames: one inward net force, tangential velocity, and release → straight-line tangent flight.

keyTerms.def: Inward acceleration v²/r = ω²r in circular motion.
Time for one complete revolution (s).
Revolutions per second, f = 1/T (Hz).
Rate of turning, ω = 2π/T = 2πf (rad/s).
Net inward force mv²/r — a role filled by real forces.
Mass circling on a string tracing a cone; tanθ = v²/rg.
Tilted road where normal force supplies the turn at design speed.

formulas.name: Circular kinematics
formulas.meaning: Speed around the loop and the inward acceleration.

formulas.name: Centripetal force
formulas.meaning: Net inward force required to sustain the circle.

workedExamples.problem: A 0.5 kg stone on a 1.2 m string whirls horizontally at 3 revolutions per second. Find its speed, centripetal acceleration and the string tension.
workedExamples.answer: 22.6 m/s, 426 m/s² inward, 213 N tension — note how fast small radii demand huge forces.

workedExamples.problem: A car rounds an unbanked curve of radius 80 m. If the tyre–road friction coefficient is 0.60, find the maximum safe speed.
workedExamples.answer: ≈22 m/s — and notice: heavy or light, same limit; grip per weight is what matters.

workedExamples.problem: A motorbike takes a frictionless banked curve at exactly its design speed of 25 m/s with bank angle 30°. Find the curve radius. (g = 9.8)
workedExamples.answer: ≈110 m — banking trades friction for geometry.

workedExamples.problem: A satellite orbits Earth at radius 7.0 × 10⁶ m with period 5,800 s. Find its orbital speed and centripetal acceleration, and compare to g at that height.
workedExamples.answer: 7.6 km/s, 8.2 m/s² — exactly the local gravitational field at that altitude: gravity IS the centripetal force; the satellite is in continuous free fall.

workedExamples.problem: Loop-the-loop: a 0.2 kg ball on a string moves in a VERTICAL circle of radius 0.8 m. Find the minimum speed at the top for the string to stay taut, and the tension there at double that speed.
workedExamples.formula: Top: mg + T = mv²/r; minimum: T = 0 → v² = gr.
workedExamples.answer: 2.8 m/s minimum; at 2× speed, tension 5.9 N (gravity covers 1/4 of the needed 7.8 N... check: mv²/r = 7.84 N total, mg = 1.96 N, string supplies the rest).

commonMistakes: Drawing an outward 'centrifugal force' on inertial-frame free-body diagrams.
Saying released objects fly radially OUTWARD — they fly off TANGENT to the circle.
Confusing v²/r (centripetal) with tangential acceleration — uniform circular motion has ZERO tangential acceleration.
Forgetting a is nonzero even though speed is constant — direction change IS acceleration.
Using degrees instead of radians in s = rθ and ω.
Loop problems: forgetting gravity contributes at the top (mg + N = mv²/r) and subtracts at the bottom (N − mg = mv²/r).
Thinking heavier vehicles need slower curves — mass cancels in µmg = mv²/r.
applications: Banked racetracks and highway curves designed with tanθ = v²/rg.
Satellites and the Moon: gravity as centripetal force — orbit = falling forever.
Washing machine spin cycle: water leaves tangentially through drum holes.
Centrifuges separate blood components by demanding more force than lighter plasma can get.
Amusement parks: loop entry speeds computed from √(gr) minimums.
Cyclists lean into turns so the ground reaction passes through their centre of mass.
g11-physics-up3-t4.summary: Circle at constant speed = acceleration v²/r INWARD (direction change). ω = 2π/T, v = ωr, a = v²/r = ω²r. Centripetal force is a ROLE: mv²/r supplied by tension/friction/gravity/normal. Banked & conical: tanθ = v²/rg. Vertical loop top: v_min = √(gr). Release → tangent, never outward.

steps: Net force must be inward: F = mv²/r
Remove the force → straight tangent path

questions.q: In uniform circular motion, the acceleration is directed:
questions.explanation: Centripetal means centre-seeking — the velocity vector's change points inward.

questions.q: Object moves in a circle r = 2 m at v = 6 m/s. Find a in m/s².
A wheel spins at 2 revolutions per second. Its angular velocity in rad/s? (Use π = 3.14)
A stone on a string breaks free. It then moves:
options: Along the tangent at the break point
questions.explanation: With no inward force, Newton's first law: straight line along the instantaneous tangent velocity.

questions.q: 1200 kg car, curve radius 60 m, speed 12 m/s. Required centripetal force (N)?
Why does the centripetal force do NO work on the object?
questions.answer: force perpendicular to velocity|F ⊥ d|no displacement along force
questions.explanation: Work = F·d·cos90° = 0 — inward force is always perpendicular to tangential motion, changing direction but not speed.

questions.q: For a car on an unbanked curve, the centripetal force is provided by:
options: Static friction between tyres and road
questions.explanation: Friction points inward at the contact patch — that's why ice (low µ) kills turns.

questions.q: Minimum speed at the top of a vertical circle of radius 0.4 m? (g = 10, v = √(gr), m/s)
An object in uniform circular motion has constant velocity.
questions.explanation: Constant SPEED, changing velocity — direction rotates continuously.
